name: vttest
why: A decades-old terminal test suite that exercises VT100 escape sequences, a sharp window into terminal history.

brief.what_it_is: vttest is a long-running interactive test program that checks how closely a terminal emulator matches DEC's VT100 and later VT-series behaviour (VT220 through VT520), plus xterm extensions. It runs inside a terminal and presents menus of test screens that a person inspects by eye, along with query/response sequences whose replies it checks. The homepage says it can also re-read its own log file as a command script, which the author used to measure coverage.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as a way to test (and demonstrate the non-compatibility of) so-called 'VT100-compatible' terminals. He began this version in 1996 to test the colour changes he was making to xterm.
brief.how_it_works: Menus are built from tables rather than case statements, which the author says makes adding entries simpler. Some tests use query/response sequences and check the replies, but most require a knowledgeable user to look at the test screen and judge the result. Extra menus and features appear only when the terminal identifies itself as a VT220 or higher, and rectangle tests only at VT420 or higher.

commands_seen.context: An xterm command-line option, quoted by the author as an example, that makes xterm identify as a VT220 so vttest shows the VT220 character-set menus. It is an xterm option, not a vttest command.

brief.install_notes: The scout's brew formula installs an executable named vttest. The homepage gives no installation steps beyond packaging. It lists packages for Debian, NetBSD pkgsrc, FreshPorts, OpenPorts, Cygwin, HP-UX, OpenCSW for Solaris, and DECUS/VMS freeware, and notes that OpenSuSE bundles it inside the xterm package. It mentions no accounts, runtimes, or configuration.
brief.standout: It is a roughly forty-year-old tool whose maintainer documents its history in detail, including how rxvt, KDE's Konsole, and the Linux and FreeBSD console drivers carried or used copies of it. It is also used to validate modern terminals such as Terminal.app and Zutty, and it is the interactive counterpart to automated tools like esctest.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage copyright runs through 2026, the page says a Konsole detail was true as of May 2026, and the author says the patch date is the effective version number. The homepage does not state a specific latest release date.
brief.caveats: The original distribution was under a noncommercial licence; the author got Per Lindberg's agreement in 2007 to move to a BSD licence. It is interactive and visual, so many results need a human to judge them. The homepage gives no platform requirements. Documentation is the source code itself plus DEC's VT100 manual, as the author states. The brew formula has no caveats.
quotes: In conformance of the good old hacker traditions, the only documentation of this program is the source code itself.
Vttest tests the compatibility (demonstrates the non-compatibility) of so-called “VT100-compatible” terminals.
fetch_log: https://invisible-island.net/vttest/ - worked; returned the full HTML project page (not a GitHub repo, so no README). Its linked subpages were not fetched; the homepage was detailed enough.

judge.reason: It turns the terminal’s hidden VT protocol into an interactive test surface, exposing the strange capabilities and incompatibilities behind everyday emulators.

entry.title: vttest
entry.tldr: A decades-old interactive test suite that puts your terminal emulator through DEC VT100-and-later escape sequences, showing how 'compatible' it really is.
entry.deeper_look:
vttest runs inside a terminal and shows a menu of test screens. Most of them draw something, such as cursor movement, screen modes or character sets, and you look at the result and judge whether your terminal got it right. Some tests send query sequences and check the replies automatically, but most need a person who knows what the screen should look like.

The author describes it as a way to test, and demonstrate the non-compatibility of, so-called "VT100-compatible" terminals. He began this version in 1996 to test colour changes he was making to xterm. The program goes well beyond the VT100: it covers the VT220 through VT520 and xterm extensions. Extra menus appear only when the terminal identifies itself as a VT220 or higher, and rectangle tests only at VT420 or higher.

The idea underneath is that a terminal is not a window that prints text. It is a state machine driven by escape sequences, and every terminal emulator you use is someone's reading of DEC's hardware from the late 1970s. vttest makes the gaps in those readings visible. Its history is documented in detail: rxvt, KDE's Konsole and the Linux and FreeBSD console drivers have carried or used copies of it, and modern terminals such as Terminal.app and Zutty have been checked against it.

The homepage notes that vttest can re-read its own log file as a command script, which the author used to measure coverage. Menus are built from tables rather than case statements, which makes adding entries simple.

try_this.what_happens: Opens the main menu of test screens; pick a number to run a test and judge by eye whether your terminal drew it correctly.

entry.whats_unique: It is a roughly forty-year-old conformance suite, still maintained, that has been used to validate real terminals and whose author documents its history in detail.
entry.caveats: Most results need a human who knows what the screen should look like, and the only documentation is the source code and DEC's VT100 manual.
